focal_region.annotated_sentence_text:
[Turn 1 USER]
e001	Our worker-owned grocery has unpredictable afternoon demand, and right now “scheduling” often means a manager sending a group message asking who can rescue the day.
e002	Some members genuinely want those hours and are annoyed when they hear about them too late.
e003	Others see the same message while collecting a child and feel they are publicly refusing the cooperative.
e004	A scheduling service says it can forecast demand and offer open shifts privately through an app.
e005	That sounds like better coordination.
e006	It also sounds like the kind of tool that calls something voluntary while quietly recording who always says yes.
e007	We need coverage, but we are a cooperative; moving all uncertainty from the store onto the people with the most flexible lives would be a strange version of efficiency.
e008	I want to know whether the service can help without turning availability into a measure of commitment.
[Turn 1 ASSISTANT]
e009	Start with control, not forecast accuracy.
e010	Protect the base schedule, make decline histories unusable for performance, offer a non-app path, and measure who receives and absorbs changes—not only whether shifts fill.
[Turn 2 USER]
e011	One correction: the pressure is already here.
e012	The base schedule is posted three weeks ahead, but the rescue messages are public.
e013	Flexible members often value them; others feel they are letting everyone down.
e014	The software might reduce that pressure—or formalize it.
[Turn 2 ASSISTANT]
e015	Agreed.
e016	The comparison is not a pressure-free status quo.
e017	Private offers may remove public refusal while a ranking rule creates a less visible hierarchy.
e018	Decide openly whether offers rotate, follow requested hours, or use another rule.
e019	Keep guaranteed hours separate, and prohibit managers from using response speed or decline frequency as a signal of commitment.
e020	The trial should ask whether pressure changed form, not merely whether the group chat became quieter.
[Turn 3 USER]
e021	Members voted to keep guaranteed weekly hours and the three-week base schedule.
e022	The service may only offer additional shifts or voluntary swaps; it cannot cancel or shorten assigned shifts.
e023	Offers will appear in the app, by text, or on a printed list in the break room.
e024	Nobody sees who declined.
e025	A rotating committee rather than the store manager will audit the offer order each week.
[Turn 3 ASSISTANT]
e026	Those rules preserve the employment baseline and make additional hours accessible through several channels.
e027	Confirm that the printed path is updated at the same time and that text or app speed does not systematically win.
e028	The committee should review outcomes, not individual willingness, and there should be a way to report pressure without raising it in a full member meeting.
[Turn 4 USER]
e029	The service can hold an offer open for thirty minutes before moving to the next person, which makes simultaneous access less important.
e030	Members can set desired extra hours and unavailable times.
e031	Two parents objected that even private offers arriving during family time feel intrusive.
e032	We added quiet hours, but a night worker says those same hours are when she wants to receive offers.
e033	One default will not fit everyone.
[Turn 4 ASSISTANT]
e034	Let members choose contact windows and channels, with no penalty for leaving them blank.
e035	A held offer should not create a race, and urgent same-day needs should be labeled separately from ordinary additions.
e036	Review whether people who set narrow windows receive fewer opportunities than they requested, because formal equality can still produce an unintended access pattern.
[Turn 5 USER]
e037	We propose an eight-week trial.
e038	The elected committee will receive weekly totals for open shifts, acceptance by channel, notice time, unfilled hours, changes in members' total hours, and anonymous reports of pressure.
e039	Managers will not see individual decline histories.
e040	The provider stores contact preferences and offer responses for the trial, then gives us an export and deletes its copy.
e041	We can return to the existing schedule without migration.
[Turn 5 ASSISTANT]
e042	The trial is bounded and does not put base hours at risk.
e043	Verify the deletion and ensure the cooperative's export does not become a permanent decline history under a different owner.
e044	Ask members before, midway, and after the trial about predictability and voluntariness, while keeping the same anonymous reporting route available throughout.
[Turn 6 USER]
e045	The committee initially proposed keeping the service if eighty percent of open shifts were filled.
e046	Members rejected a single threshold.
e047	The final review will look at coverage alongside notice, distribution of extra hours, reported pressure, and whether people received the opportunities they requested.
e048	Any member can propose stopping early, and a majority vote can pause offers while the committee investigates.
[Turn 6 ASSISTANT]
e049	That matches the cooperative's purpose better than optimizing one staffing measure.
e050	Write the review questions before launch and publish weekly summaries so concerns do not depend on access to the committee.
e051	The pause route is proportionate because the base schedule continues even if the offer system stops.
[Turn 7 USER]
e052	We will run the eight weeks with guaranteed hours untouched, member-selected contact windows, thirty-minute offers, equal channel timing, private declines, committee auditing, anonymous reporting, and the member pause vote.
e053	At the end, members will review both operational results and their own experience before deciding whether to keep it.
e054	The managers know they cannot use the trial to judge who is committed to the cooperative.
[Turn 7 ASSISTANT]
e055	This is ready for an eight-week trial.
e056	Members retain guaranteed schedules, choose contact windows, decline privately, audit offer order through an elected committee, and can pause a system whose disappearance would not remove base hours.
e057	The review also looks beyond fill rate to distribution, notice, and experienced pressure.
e058	If the channels truly receive equal notice, the design tests coordination without redefining flexibility as obligation.
e059	Preserve weekly results and let the member vote—not manager enthusiasm or vendor convenience—decide what follows.
[Turn 8 USER]
e060	The equal-notice assumption failed before we assigned a single shift.
e061	In the dry test, texts arrived minutes after app alerts for some members.
e062	The provider can start the thirty-minute clock after digital delivery, but a paper list cannot confirm anything.
e063	People who use the break-room list asked why a routine shift has to move through the rotation in half an hour at all.
e064	So our “multiple channels” design still gave the app first access.
e065	We had a fairness rule in the policy and a race in the mechanics.
[Turn 8 ASSISTANT]
e066	Then my readiness condition was not met.
e067	Split routine from genuine same-day emergencies.
e068	Routine offers can remain open long enough for the printed path and then use the transparent rotation; urgent offers may use faster channels but need separate reporting.
e069	Watch the category itself—if more work becomes “urgent,” the accessible route will disappear without any formal rule changing.
[Turn 9 USER]
e070	Some members objected that rotation ignores who has repeatedly helped during shortages.
e071	They want reliable volunteers to receive earlier offers.
e072	Others said that would turn past availability into a permanent advantage and punish people whose circumstances change.
e073	Because we own the store together, contribution matters, but I agree the scheduling system should not become an informal loyalty score.
[Turn 9 ASSISTANT]
e074	Keep recognition and shift allocation separate.
e075	If the cooperative wants to recognize emergency contributions, decide that openly through compensation, time off, or another member policy.
e076	For access to paid hours, use requested hours and rotation with visible rules.
e077	Otherwise a scheduling convenience will create an employment hierarchy without a governance decision.
[Turn 10 USER]
e078	The pre-trial survey revealed another tension.
e079	Members asking for the most additional hours are already concentrated in two lower-paid roles.
e080	Filling their requests improves income, but it may also make the cooperative rely on chronic overtime-like availability instead of adding a regular position.
e081	The store manager says we should first learn whether demand is stable enough to hire.
e082	The members involved say extra shifts are useful now and should not be withheld to make a staffing point.
[Turn 10 ASSISTANT]
e083	Offer the hours now, but track recurring gaps by role and trigger a separate staffing review.
e084	Do not deny current income; do not call a permanent labor need optional forever because someone keeps accepting it.
[Turn 11 USER]
e085	Managers now want decline reasons during holiday weeks.
e086	Their example is reasonable: if five people refuse late closing because there is no transport home, an aggregate “unavailable” does not help them solve it.
e087	Members hear a database explaining why each of them said no, which could become a dossier even if nobody intends that today.
e088	The committee offered voluntary aggregate reasons.
e089	Managers say aggregate data cannot arrange a ride for a specific person.
e090	Members say a person who wants help can ask for help without explaining every refusal.
e091	I support that distinction, but I also do not want privacy to become a ceremonial principle that prevents the cooperative from fixing a barrier people actually want fixed.
[Turn 11 ASSISTANT]
e092	Provide a voluntary route to request a concrete accommodation or suggest a barrier, separate from declining a shift.
e093	Managers can act on aggregate patterns and on member-initiated cases without receiving a history that can influence later judgments.
e094	Review whether the route produces fixes; if it does not, the committee can adjust it with members rather than expanding surveillance by default.
[Turn 12 USER]
e095	The eight-week trial will now distinguish routine and urgent offers, keep routine offers open for the printed channel, allocate paid hours by requested-hours rotation, and trigger a separate staffing review when recurring gaps cross the prewritten threshold.
e096	Decline histories remain private, while members can voluntarily request help with a barrier.
e097	Guaranteed schedules, quiet windows, committee auditing, weekly distribution reports, the pause vote, and the final member decision all remain.
e098	The dry run changed the mechanics without changing who controls them.
[Turn 12 ASSISTANT]
e099	The expanded design addresses four different problems without asking the software to decide what fairness means: unequal channel timing, an informal loyalty score, recurring hours that may really be a permanent job, and the difference between offering help and collecting explanations for refusal.
e100	Preserve the failed dry run, not just the corrected settings.
e101	Keep routine and urgent offer counts separate, record the requested-hours rotation, show when the staffing threshold fires, and retain anonymous reports alongside operational totals.
e102	The final member vote should be able to see whether coverage improved, who received additional income, who absorbed short notice, and whether declining remained genuinely consequence-free.
e103	If those answers conflict, the cooperative—not a fill-rate target—owns the trade-off.

packet.question: How did the working position or decision change, and does any unresolved qualification remain capable of changing it?
